caption:
Were the Cottingley Fairies real? No. Two girls faked them with cardboard cutouts and hatpins — and it took them 66 years to say so.

In mid-1917, nine-year-old Frances Griffiths was staying with her aunt in Cottingley, near Bradford. She and her 16-year-old cousin Elsie Wright kept coming home from the beck with wet feet. They said they went there to see the fairies, and borrowed Elsie's father's Midg quarter-plate camera to prove it. They came back about 30 minutes later, "triumphant".

Arthur Wright developed the plate himself and dismissed the figures as cardboard cutouts. Elsie was artistic and had worked in a photographer's studio. He searched their bedroom and the beck and found nothing incriminating.

By 1920 the pictures had reached Sir Arthur Conan Doyle, who used them in The Strand's Christmas issue. The issue sold out within days. The photography expert Harold Snelling called the negatives "entirely genuine, unfaked photographs". Kodak refused a certificate of authenticity. Ilford reported "some evidence of faking".

In 1983 the cousins confessed. Elsie had copied Claude Shepperson's dancing fairies from Princess Mary's Gift Book of 1914 — a book Frances had brought from South Africa — changed few details and added wings. They propped the cutouts up with hatpins and threw them in the beck afterwards.

Still unresolved: the fifth photograph. Elsie said it was fake like the rest. Frances insisted she saw fairies building up in the grass and simply aimed the camera. Both claimed to have taken it. Geoffrey Crawley suggested an unintended double exposure — which would let both women be sincere.

Images: four of the five Cottingley photographs by Elsie Wright and Frances Griffiths, 1917 and 1920; Conan Doyle in The Strand, 1920; Claude Shepperson's illustration from Princess Mary's Gift Book, 1914. All public domain.
